strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across three knowledge-intensive VQA benchmarks (InfoSeek, OK-VQA, Encyclopedic VQA) with both retrieval recall and answer accuracy, showing competitive or state-of-the-art results, particularly strong cross-benchmark generalization compared to prior methods that trade off across datasets.

Careful ablation design: component-wise ablation (multi-query, heterogeneous KB, iteration), iteration-count analysis, top-k sensitivity, retriever-scaling analysis, and model-allocation analysis (Appendix G) with retrieval budgets held constant, which strengthens the empirical case that iteration is the main driver of gains.

Reasonable effort toward reproducibility: full prompt templates, downsampling procedure, retrieval implementation details (embedding construction, FAISS indexing), few-shot prompting for EM, and a computational cost analysis are provided in appendices.

The lightweight-retriever setup (SigLIP2-SO400m + ModernBERT, E5-base) is deliberately chosen over strong specialized retrievers to isolate the contribution of the iterative reasoning loop, which is methodologically commendable.
The framework is training-free and modular, making it practically useful and easy to adopt on top of existing retrievers and MLLMs.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core loop (query expansion, sub-query generation, iterative retrieve-reason with accumulated context) is a direct adaptation of well-established text-domain iterative RAG (IRCoT, Self-RAG, RA-ISF, etc.). The multimodal extensions — multi-query across two KBs, a fixed image-to-image similarity term — are sensible but incremental combinations of known techniques rather than new mechanisms.

Metric comparability concerns in the headline retrieval tables: the full framework reports cumulative recall after 4 iterations using multiple queries per iteration (Table 1, R@5-only), which is not directly comparable to baselines' single-shot R@10/R@20. The vanilla baseline's 'average recall across iterations' is also an unusual, non-standard metric. This weakens the strength of claimed retrieval superiority.

Heavy dependence on closed-source frontier models (Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o) for headline results, and inconsistent answerer configurations across tables (some rows use Gemini-generated reasoning records with third-party checkpoints, others self-generate), which complicates fair comparison and reproducibility; no code release is mentioned.

Very high inference cost: ~147 s/sample by iteration 3 (Appendix E), with retrieval time itself growing super-linearly; no end-to-end cost comparison against single-pass baselines is provided, so the accuracy-per-compute trade-off of the iterative approach remains unquantified.

Cover EM is adopted as the 'primary metric' for ablations partly because the model produces long rationales; CEM can be inflated by verbose outputs that mention many candidate answers, and this metric switch directionally favors the proposed method. The justification is plausible but the risk of metric gaming is not analyzed.

OK-VQA retrieval uses Pseudo-Relevance Recall (a proxy metric, since no ground-truth annotations exist), which is weaker evidence than the entity-recall results elsewhere; also, the multimodal KB is drawn from Encyclopedic VQA's own image-text collection, and potential overlap/leakage considerations for the EncVQA evaluation are not explicitly discussed.

Ablations are run on ~500-question downsampled subsets with no variance estimates or significance testing anywhere in the paper, so it is hard to judge whether small reported deltas (e.g., +1.9% accuracy from retriever scaling) are meaningful.

Presentation issues reduce polish: e.g., 'Gemma-4' instead of Gemma-3-4B in Section 6.3, mismatched citation formatting ('Changin et al.'), inconsistent table symbols, and the R@5-only reporting for the full framework without explanation of why R@10/R@20 cumulative recall is omitted.

strengths: The paper is positioned at a relevant and timely intersection for the ACL community (iterative/agentive RAG applied to multimodal, knowledge-intensive VQA), and the motivation for why a single-pass retrieve-then-read loop is insufficient is articulated clearly.

The experimental coverage is broad: three standard benchmarks (InfoSeek, Encyclopedic VQA, OK-VQA), both retrieval recall and answer accuracy, comparisons against many recent baselines, and component ablations (multi-query, heterogeneous KB, iterations), plus analyses of retriever scaling and top-k sensitivity.

The appendix provides unusually detailed implementation material (prompt templates, KB construction, downsampling procedure, computational cost per iteration), which supports reproducibility of the pipeline.
The ablations are conducted under a controlled retrieval budget, which is a fair attempt to isolate the contribution of the iterative reasoning components from sheer retrieval volume.
The lightweight-retriever design choice (SigLIP2 + ModernBERT + E5) is a sensible attempt to show gains are not solely due to a heavy retriever.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core mechanism (query expansion + sub-query generation + iterative summarization of retrieved evidence into a running record) is a direct port of well-established text-domain iterative RAG techniques (IRCoT, Self-RAG-style loops, FLARE, RA-ISF) to the multimodal setting. The multimodal-specific additions — a concatenated image+text embedding for retrieval and heterogeneous KBs — are engineering contributions rather than a new methodology, and the paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond adaptation.

Baseline comparisons are substantially confounded by model scale and access. Headline accuracy results (e.g., 75.5% on Encyclopedic VQA, 51.7% on InfoSeek) rely on Gemini-2.5-Flash or GPT-4o as the reasoner/answerer, while most compared baselines use 7-8B open models, many of them fine-tuned. The 'state-of-the-art' claims therefore conflate the framework's contribution with frontier proprietary model capability. The Gemma-3-4B rows partially mitigate this, but even those use an instruction-tuned modern MLLM against older baselines, and the vanilla/full distinction is murky in Table 1 (cumulative recall over 4 iterations vs. single-pass baselines; different effective retrieval budgets).

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or repeated runs are reported anywhere, despite the ablations being run on downsampled subsets of only ~500 examples, where differences of a few points may not be meaningful. Several claimed gains (e.g., Table 4 in the appendix, the model-allocation analysis) are within ranges that could be noise on such subsets.

The Cover EM metric choice is justified by claiming models produce correct rationales before the final answer, but CEM can reward verbosity and hallucination-adjacent behavior; reporting CEM as the 'primary metric' for ablations while prior work is compared under stricter EM weakens comparability, and no human verification of CEM correctness is provided.

Reproducibility depends on closed, versioned commercial APIs (Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o via OpenRouter), whose behavior changes over time; no code release or artifact commitment is mentioned, so exact reproduction of the reported numbers is not feasible.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: Table 1's caption discusses 'accuracies' though it reports recall; Section 6.3 refers to 'Gemma-4' (nonexistent model); the multimodal similarity scoring method is attributed to 'Changin et al. (2025)', which is a paper on retrieval-augmented audio captioning, and the citation key/name appears garbled; there are numerous grammatical errors ('To acquire the a diverse set', 'In this stage, MLLM', 'a analysis further explored'). These suggest the paper was not carefully proofread.

The paper does not analyze failure modes, error propagation through iterations (e.g., what happens when the reasoning record contains wrong information), or cases where iteration hurts; the claim that gains 'saturate' is based on a single-dataset curve (Figure 2) and the computational cost grows substantially per iteration (over 145 seconds per sample by iteration 3), which is acknowledged only briefly.

The evaluation of retrieval on OK-VQA uses Pseudo-Relevance Recall, a proxy metric that inflates apparent quality relative to ground-truth recall used elsewhere; combining different metric regimes across tables makes cross-benchmark claims of consistency hard to verify.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper clearly articulates why single-pass retrieve-then-read RAG is insufficient for knowledge-intensive VQA (need for multi-facet visual entity grounding and cross-modal compositional reasoning), and positions iterative RAG against this gap.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three established knowledge-intensive VQA benchmarks (InfoSeek, Encyclopedic VQA, OK-VQA) with multiple retrieval and accuracy metrics, showing consistent gains over prior methods.

Carefully controlled ablations: component ablation (multi-query, heterogeneous KB, iteration) with a strictly controlled retrieval budget (Table 6), iteration-wise analysis (Table 7), KB configuration ablation (Table 8), and top-k sensitivity (Table 9) that honestly reports when more context hurts weaker models (Gemma degradation at k=20).

Emphasis on a lightweight retriever setup (SigLIP2-SO400m + ModernBERT, E5-base) to isolate the contribution of iterative reasoning from brute-force retrieval strength, plus an explicit analysis of scaling both MLLM (Appendix G) and retriever (Section 6.1).
Practical cost analysis (Appendix E) and complete prompt templates (Appendix A) support transparency of the framework's operation.
The few-shot prompting protocol, downsampling procedure for ablation subsets, and retrieval implementation details in the appendix improve reproducibility of the experimental setup.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness concerns in the headline tables: the strongest results use Gemini-2.5-Flash or GPT-4o, while most fine-tuned baselines use 7B-scale models; the SOTA claims (Tables 3-4) are substantially driven by the answerer model's capacity rather than the framework alone. The non-Apple-Lens rows in Table 3 also mix very different retrieval conditions (Google Lens vs. own retriever), complicating direct comparison.

Retrieval comparisons use a cumulative-recall protocol over 4 iterations (i.e., much larger total retrieval budget) against single-pass baselines; while the vanilla baseline partially addresses this, the cross-method recall numbers in Tables 1-2 are not strictly budget-matched, which inflates apparent advantages.

Metric inconsistency across benchmarks (BEM on Encyclopedic VQA, EM with few-shot training examples on InfoSeek, VQA-score/Cover-EM on OK-VQA) complicates interpretation; the few-shot EM setup uses training-split examples including ground-truth answers, which is a non-trivial protocol choice that needs more justification.

Novelty is moderate: the method is largely a careful adaptation of text-domain iterative RAG (query expansion + sub-question generation + reasoning accumulation) to the multimodal setting; the multimodal retrieval component is borrowed (Changin et al., 2025), and no new modeling or training contribution is introduced.
No statement of code or artifact release, and heavy reliance on closed-source API models (Gemini, GPT-4o) limits independent verification of the headline results.

Minor polish issues remain: typos/inconsistencies (e.g., 'Gemma-4' vs Gemma-3-4B in Section 6.3, 'MIRAG' vs 'MI-RAG'), duplicate prompt numbering in Appendix A, and the ablations on ~500-question downsampled subsets limit statistical strength; no error analysis or qualitative failure case study is provided.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six diverse knowledge-intensive VQA benchmarks (InfoSeek, E-VQA, OK-VQA, FVQA-test, MMSearch, LiveVQA), covering both fixed-KB and open-web settings, which supports the claimed generality of the framework.

The framework is clearly specified and training-free: dual-scope query formulation, heterogeneous KB retrieval, record synthesis, and adaptive termination are formalized with equations, and all prompt templates are provided in the appendix, making the approach reproducible in principle.

Ablations are unusually thorough: component ablation (Table 6), per-iteration performance with fixed trajectory (Table 5), adaptive termination vs. fixed budget (Table 7), retriever scaling, top-k sensitivity, interpolation weight λ, and a controlled distractor/noise sensitivity analysis (Table A8) that credibly isolates the effect of contextual noise.

The trajectory-type analysis (Tables 8, 9, and Appendix N) provides a genuinely informative behavioral comparison against an agentic baseline (WebWatcher) under the same KB and retriever, supporting the claim of reduced error propagation rather than merely reporting final scores.

Careful experimental hygiene in places: perceptual-hash deduplication of the KB against evaluation splits, a controlled answerer (LLaVA-MORE-8B) on InfoSeek to isolate the contribution of the reasoning trajectory, and per-iteration/KB-level recall analysis in the appendix.
weaknesses: The headline retrieval comparison is not apples-to-apples: PMSR is compared against single-pass baselines using cumulative recall (union of evidence accumulated over up to 5 iterations, each retrieving 20 texts + 10 image-text pairs), while baselines report R@k for a single retrieval pass. This inflates PMSR's apparent advantage in Tables 1 and 2; per-iteration recall is relegated to the appendix, and a single-pass baseline with an equivalent total retrieval budget is not reported in the main tables.

End-to-end accuracy claims are weakened by backbone asymmetry: with the open-source Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, PMSR (41.5 on InfoSeek, 46.4 on E-VQA) is at or below the strongest baselines (OMGM†: 43.5 / 50.2-51.2). The 'surpassing by 8.7%' claim on E-VQA relies on substituting Gemini-2.5-Flash as the trajectory generator, a substantially more capable proprietary model, which conflates the framework's contribution with backbone strength.

On MMSearch, PMSR (54.3) clearly trails DeepEyesV2 (63.7), and the abstract/introduction's claim of 'outstanding performance on five benchmarks' overstates a mixed picture; the narrative would benefit from more precise scoping of where the method does and does not win.

No statement about code or data release is provided, and no statistical significance testing or variance reporting accompanies the main results; combined with reliance on GPT-4o-based LLM-as-Judge for several benchmarks, reproducibility of the exact numbers is uncertain.

Novelty is moderate: the core idea—iterative, reasoning-guided retrieval with accumulated state—is well established in text-only iterative RAG (RAT, IRCoT, Auto-RAG, FLARE-style methods), and the paper's contribution is primarily an adaptation of this recipe to multimodal KBs plus a record/trajectory conditioning scheme; the positioning against this line of work could be sharper.

Some design choices are under-justified: each record is generated solely from newly retrieved candidates without conditioning on prior records (Eq. 8), the fixed λ=0.5 conflicts with the appendix finding that λ=0.3-0.4 performs best, and the evidence-usage gap noted in Section 6.1 (records correct but answers wrong) is observed but only partially explained.

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: evaluation spans six knowledge-intensive VQA benchmarks (both KB-based and search-oriented), with multiple backbones (Qwen3-VL-4B/8B, Gemini-2.5-Flash), which is more extensive than many multimodal RAG papers.

The framework is clearly described, with the trajectory-of-compact-records design separating retrieval/refinement from final answer generation; the controlled setup on InfoSeek (fixed LLaVA-MORE-8B answerer regardless of trajectory generator) is a thoughtful attempt to isolate the framework's contribution.

Substantial ablation and analysis: component ablation (Table 6), per-iteration dynamics (Table 5), adaptive termination analysis (Tables 7, 9), trajectory-type analysis (Table 8), retriever scaling, top-k and lambda sensitivity, and a distractor-sensitivity study in the appendix.

The adaptive termination criterion is simple, well-motivated (query saturation), and its cost/accuracy trade-off is honestly reported (Table 7), including that adaptive stopping slightly underperforms fixed 5 iterations.
Detailed appendices (prompts, deduplication of KB images against eval splits via perceptual hashing, computational cost analysis) improve reproducibility of the described setup.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: PMSR is an engineering combination of well-established ideas — iterative/IRCoT-style query decomposition, self-reflection RAG, memory compaction, and coarse-to-fine heterogeneous retrieval. The 'record-level query' is implemented as simple concatenation [Q; r_{t-1}], and the 'trajectory-level query' is a prompt; the core algorithmic contribution is thin for a main-conference paper.

The headline retrieval comparisons are potentially unfair. PMSR's 'cumulative recall' aggregates candidates across up to 5 iterations (roughly 5x the single-pass budget) yet is directly compared against baselines' single-pass R@5/R@10/R@20. Per-iteration recall relegated to Appendix A2 (e.g., E-VQA heterogeneous KB 58.5 at iteration 1, vs. OMGM† R@20 of 58.7) suggests that at a comparable budget PMSR's retrieval is not clearly superior; the main-table claims rest largely on the inflated cumulative budget.

Accuracy results are mixed and selectively presented: on the full InfoSeek validation set PMSR reports no result ('-' in Table 3), and the reported M2KR-subset results (38.3/41.5) trail OMGM† (43.5); the 'substantial improvement' narrative relies on the Gemini-2.5-Flash configuration (50.5) and on a fixed external answerer for EM. The best numbers throughout depend on a proprietary model, weakening reproducibility and the fairness of comparisons.

Baseline comparability is loose across tables: different retrievers (SigLIP2-g vs. EVA-CLIP-8B vs. PreFLMR), different answer models (LLaVA-1.5 vs. GPT-4o vs. Qwen variants), and in Table 4, RL-trained search agents are compared against a training-free pipeline on only some benchmarks; on MMSearch PMSR (54.3) is clearly worse than DeepEyesV2 (63.7), which the text soft-pedals as 'competitive.'

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting for any comparison; several claimed margins are small (e.g., Table 4 FVQA 61.2 vs. 60.6, LiveVQA 54.2 vs. 51.2, InfoSeek Human 58.2 vs. 55.1).

The record-synthesis design (each record generated only from newly retrieved candidates, not conditioned on prior records) risks discarding previously acquired correct evidence, and the paper does not analyze this failure mode; the acknowledged gap between record correctness (>70% Stable-Correct+Correction on E-VQA) and final accuracy is not resolved, only further diagnosed.
No statement of code or artifact release; combined with the proprietary-model configurations and under-specified judge evaluation (GPT-4o LLM-as-Judge), independent reproduction is difficult.

Occasional overstatement in the narrative ('outstanding performance on five benchmarks', 'consistently and substantially improves') that is not fully supported by the tables as a whole, particularly when like-for-like budgets and backbones are considered.

strengths: The paper is well organized and clearly written, with the method (initial record generation, dual-scope queries, record synthesis, adaptive termination) specified in enough detail (including prompts in Appendix A and retrieval implementation in Appendix D) to support reproducibility.

Evaluation coverage is broad: six knowledge-intensive VQA benchmarks spanning encyclopedic (E-VQA, InfoSeek), open-domain (MMSearch, LiveVQA, InfoSeek Human), and knowledge-grounded (OK-VQA, FVQA) settings, with two open-source backbone tiers plus a proprietary model to probe scaling.

The ablation study (Table 6) cleanly separates the contributions of heterogeneous KBs, dual-scope queries, and iterative refinement, and per-iteration analysis (Table 5, Appendix G) shows where gains arise.

The trajectory-type analysis (Tables 8-9, Appendix N) is a thoughtful addition: it goes beyond headline accuracy to characterize error correction vs. drift, and the WebWatcher comparison under a matched KB/retriever gives evidence for the claimed stability benefit of record-based updating.

The sensitivity analyses (top-k, retriever scaling, interpolation weight λ, distractor noise in Appendix M) are above-average in rigor and the distractor analysis (oracle + retrieved context degrading from 86.6% to 72.5%) is an interesting and honest finding.
Practical details such as KB deduplication against evaluation splits via perceptual hashing and a computational cost analysis (Appendix P) increase trustworthiness.
weaknesses: The headline retrieval comparison is not apples-to-apples. PMSR reports cumulative recall over ~3.3 adaptive iterations (roughly 60-100 retrieved candidates accumulated across record- and trajectory-level queries), while baselines report R@5/10/20. Comparing cumulative multi-iteration recall against fixed-budget R@20 substantially inflates the apparent margin (e.g., 93.9 vs. 86.4 on InfoSeek). A fixed-budget or per-iteration comparison against baselines in the main table is needed.

The end-to-end accuracy comparison is confounded by backbone strength. Most baselines use LLaVA-1.5-7B, Mistral-7B, or similar, whereas PMSR's best results use Qwen3-VL-8B and Gemini-2.5-Flash. The fixed-answerer protocol on InfoSeek partially addresses this, but the trajectory generator itself is a much stronger model, so the claimed improvements cannot be cleanly attributed to the framework.

Several core components are relatively simple prompting strategies (query concatenation, summarize-and-append records, similarity-based stopping). The paper would benefit from sharper positioning against closely related iterative/text RAG methods (e.g., RAT, FLARE, IRCoT-style interleaving, EchoSight) to establish what is genuinely new beyond applying known iteration ideas to multimodal retrieval.

Reproducibility is only partial. The web-equipped variant depends on commercial APIs (Google Lens via ScrapingDog, Ollama Web Search, GPT-OSS summarizer) and LLM-as-Judge uses GPT-4o, making exact replication difficult; no code release is stated.

No statistical significance testing or variance estimates are reported anywhere, despite many margins being modest (e.g., 46.4 vs. 47.1 for adaptive vs. fixed termination; 46.3 vs. 46.4 in the top-k study).

The paper mixes evaluation protocols across benchmarks (EM, BEM, CEM, LLM-as-Judge) without cross-metric consistency, and E-VQA results are restricted to the single-hop subset, limiting comparability with works reporting the full set.

Some claims exceed the evidence: 'outstanding performance on five benchmarks' rests partly on the non-comparable cumulative recall metric, and the conclusion that adaptive termination reduces error propagation is supported only indirectly by the trajectory-type counts.
